> **TL;DR:** In this small, single-split benchmark, Kumo had the best raw-feature score on five of six datasets. With engineered features, tuned classical models led on Iris and Diabetes, while Kumo remained competitive elsewhere. Treat these as dataset-specific results—not a general ranking—and validate them with repeated splits. Better data, an understandable model or cheaper predictions may matter more than a small improvement in the score.

Can a pretrained tabular model compete with modestly tuned classical models? And does adding domain knowledge through feature engineering change the result?

To explore those questions, I compared NVIDIA's Kumo-Tabular with Gradient Boosting, Histogram Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, CatBoost and, for classification, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Each dataset was evaluated twice: first with its original features, then with a small set of domain-inspired features added.

This is a small, single-split experiment—not a universal ranking. It compares predictive performance under one clearly specified evaluation protocol; it does not establish a general winner.

There is also a bigger question behind the comparison: is choosing a more powerful model actually the next useful step? In practice, I might ask for better data, fit a regression I can explain, or choose a model that is cheap enough to serve millions of predictions. The benchmark cannot settle those decisions, but they belong in the discussion.

## What is Kumo-Tabular?

Kumo-Tabular is a pretrained Transformer for structured data. It uses labeled rows as context when predicting targets for new rows. This is a form of **in-context learning**: unlike conventional models, Kumo does not update its weights to fit Iris, Wine, Diabetes or the other benchmark datasets.

According to [NVIDIA's model card](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Tabular) and [technical overview](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/kumo-tabular), Kumo-Tabular was pretrained entirely on synthetic tables generated from structural causal models. During pretraining, it learned to predict labels for held-out rows given labeled context rows. NVIDIA reports that the Small model used here saw around 35 million synthetic tables.

At prediction time, Kumo returns class probabilities for classification and 999 quantiles for regression. For regression in this benchmark, I used the median quantile, `q500`, as the point prediction.

The distinction is important: Kumo arrives with substantial pretraining, while the other models learn from each dataset's training split. This comparison asks how they perform under the setup below; it does not equalize compute or training history.

## Does synthetic pretraining prevent leakage?

If NVIDIA's description applies to this checkpoint, synthetic pretraining reduces concern that the model directly memorized real benchmark rows during pretraining. It is not, however, an independent audit or a guarantee that an evaluation is leakage-free.

In this notebook, Kumo receives training labels as context, not held-out test labels, and the classical models are tuned on training folds only. Even so, related or duplicate records crossing a split, features containing future information, or repeatedly choosing models based on test scores can make results optimistic. Appropriate time- or group-based splits and a genuinely held-out final evaluation still matter.

## What about relational databases?

The Kumo family also includes [Kumo-Relational](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational), a separate pretrained model designed for related tables. For example, a churn prediction can use customers, orders and products linked by keys: the model exchanges information across those relationships through graph-based message passing. This is particularly relevant when predictive signals span tables and can reduce the need to manually flatten a database or build aggregates.

NVIDIA also describes Kumo-Relational as pretrained on synthetic relational data; the **35 million tables** figure above refers specifically to Kumo-Tabular Small. The relational model still requires appropriate tables, relationships and prediction-time cutoffs. Our notebook evaluates only Kumo-Tabular on flat, single-table datasets, so its results do not establish how Kumo-Relational performs on a database.

## Before choosing a model, look at the data

These datasets arrive as ready-to-use tables. Most real projects do not. Before comparing algorithms, I would check what each row represents, how the target was recorded, whether units are consistent, and which records are missing or duplicated. A model can learn an error in the data just as readily as a useful pattern.

At the beginning of a project, a data scientist may still be able to change what gets collected. That is worth discussing with the people who own the process:

- **Ask for more useful observations.** If failures or particular customer groups are underrepresented, collect more of those cases or improve their labels. More rows from the same narrow sample will not necessarily fix the problem.
- **Look for missing information, not just missing values.** Weather, product attributes or historical activity from another source might explain variation that the current table cannot. Check coverage, permissions, join keys and units before adding it. A one-to-many join can accidentally duplicate observations.
- **Keep the prediction time in view.** An extra column is only useful for deployment if it will be available when the prediction is made. Historical joins need the information available at that time, not a later revision.

Adding a second source is different from deriving petal area from two existing columns: it can bring genuinely new information. Neither approach guarantees an improvement, so both need evaluation on an appropriate held-out split. Any learned imputation, scaling or encoding must be fitted on training data only.

This benchmark keeps the observations fixed and changes their representation. It does **not** test whether collecting more data, improving labels or enriching the tables would help more than switching models. Even "raw" here means the prepared input columns, not untouched source data.

## Benchmark setup

| Task | Datasets | Models |
|---|---|---|
| Classification | Iris, Wine, Breast Cancer | Kumo, Gradient Boosting, Histogram Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, CatBoost, LDA |
| Regression | Diabetes, Air Quality (ozone), Auto MPG | Kumo, Gradient Boosting, Histogram Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, CatBoost |

Each dataset uses one fixed 75/25 train/test split (seed 42), stratified for classification. Raw and engineered scenarios use the same split. Each classical model—including XGBoost, CatBoost and LDA—is tuned with Optuna for **5 trials**, using five-fold cross-validation on the training split only. The selected model is refit on the full training split and evaluated once on the test data. LDA uses standardization inside the cross-validation pipeline, preventing the scaler from learning from validation or test rows. Kumo uses its pretrained weights without dataset-specific weight updates or hyperparameter search.

The engineered scenario adds domain-inspired features: examples include petal area for Iris, horsepower-to-weight for Auto MPG, and BMI multiplied by blood pressure for Diabetes. The same scenario-specific columns are supplied to every model, including Kumo. These features are computed independently for each row; no transformation is learned from the test split. For Auto MPG, the engineered scenario also replaces the numeric origin code with one-hot indicators.

All conclusions are limited to this one held-out split. Its test set is small, so a few predictions can move the results noticeably.

## Results

For classification, the primary metric is **log loss**; lower is better. Kumo's raw-feature accuracy is included for context. The scores below come from one test split; the small differences should not be read as stable rankings.

| Dataset | Raw best (log loss) | Kumo raw accuracy | Engineered best (log loss) | Kumo engineered log loss |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| Iris | Kumo (0.0571) | 100.0% | LDA (0.0838) | 0.0880 |
| Wine | Histogram Gradient Boosting (0.0030) | 100.0% | Histogram Gradient Boosting (0.0032) | 0.0191 |
| Breast Cancer | Kumo (0.0620) | 97.9% | Kumo (0.0586) | 0.0586 |

For regression, the primary metric is **RMSE**; lower is better. Values use each dataset's target units. Since Kumo uses its median prediction (`q500`), its MAE is also shown; lower MAE is naturally aligned with a median forecast.

| Dataset | Raw best (RMSE) | Engineered best (RMSE) | Kumo RMSE, raw → engineered | Kumo MAE, raw → engineered |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| Diabetes | Kumo (51.77) | Gradient Boosting (51.17) | 51.77 → 52.43 | 39.88 → 40.35 |
| Air Quality | Kumo (24.17) | Kumo (22.88) | 24.17 → 22.88 | 17.54 → 16.30 |
| Auto MPG | Kumo (2.13) | Kumo (2.19) | 2.13 → 2.19 | 1.45 → 1.48 |

## What stands out

On the raw features, Kumo had the lowest primary metric on **five of six datasets**; Histogram Gradient Boosting led on Wine. That is a result for this split and this five-trial search, not evidence that Kumo generally wins on raw tables.

With engineered features, Kumo had the lowest observed score on three of six datasets (Breast Cancer, Air Quality and Auto MPG). LDA led on Iris, Histogram Gradient Boosting on Wine, and Gradient Boosting on Diabetes.

Feature engineering did not help Kumo uniformly on this split: its primary score improved on Wine, Breast Cancer and Air Quality, but worsened on Iris, Diabetes and Auto MPG. For example, Iris log loss moved from 0.057 to 0.088, while Air Quality RMSE moved from 24.17 to 22.88. These before/after differences are descriptive, not causal estimates of feature engineering: the engineered scenario adds columns and, for Auto MPG, changes how origin is represented.

Accuracy can conceal probability-quality differences. On Wine, all six models reached 100% accuracy on the raw split, yet their log-loss values differed; in the engineered scenario, five of six did so. Log loss reflects the confidence assigned to predictions, not just whether the top class was correct.

## When explaining the result matters more

The best predictive score is not always the objective. Sometimes I need to explain how an outcome is associated with a few measured variables, report uncertainty, or give someone a model they can inspect without another explanation tool.

For that task, a carefully specified **linear regression can be a better choice** than Kumo or boosting, even if its prediction error is higher. Its coefficients describe conditional associations in the chosen model, and its assumptions can be examined with diagnostics. For a binary outcome, logistic regression offers a similar starting point. Linear models can also be competitive predictors when the signal is simple or the sample is small.

That does not make a coefficient a causal effect. Confounding, correlated predictors, measurement error and model misspecification can all undermine an interpretation. Explaining why a fitted model produced a prediction is also different from explaining why something happened in the world. Feature-attribution tools for complex models do not remove that distinction.

I did not include linear regression in this benchmark; LDA is a classifier, not a substitute for that comparison. These tables therefore say nothing about whether a well-specified regression would be adequate for an explanatory task.

## A good notebook result still has to fit the service

When I worked at Allegro with massive amounts of metadata, we needed simpler models that were fast to compute. At that scale, the cost of each prediction mattered. A small gain in an offline metric was not the whole decision.

The same trade-off matters in high-volume services such as recommendation or ranking at Netflix or Amazon—not as a claim about their particular model choices, but as a deployment constraint. How many items need scoring, how often, and within what latency budget?

Kumo avoids dataset-specific weight training, but that does not make inference free. Running a Transformer over labeled context is more computationally demanding than evaluating a small linear model. Its practical cost relative to a particular boosting model depends on context size, hardware, batching and caching. Pretraining shifts work away from fitting each new dataset; it does not eliminate prediction-time work.

Before deploying it, I would measure throughput, memory use, cost per prediction and tail latency under realistic load, with model loading separated from warm inference. Batch scoring might make a heavier model entirely practical; a strict per-request latency budget might favor a simpler one. **This notebook does not measure those production trade-offs**, so its accuracy results are not evidence that Kumo is either suitable or unsuitable for a high-demand service.

## Limitations

This is a **small benchmark, not a definitive leaderboard**. There is one train/test split per dataset, and test sets contain only 28–143 observations. A few predictions can move a score noticeably. The five-trial tuning budget is deliberately modest and is not exhaustive optimization. Classical models receive dataset-specific fitting and tuning; Kumo instead benefits from external pretraining. The compute budgets are not matched.

The comparison should be validated with repeated splits before making stronger claims. Selecting a best model from several tuned alternatives on one held-out split can make small score differences look more meaningful than they are.

There are also dataset-specific constraints. The Air Quality data uses complete cases only: 111 of 153 rows. Its random split tests interpolation among days from the same season, not forecasting into the future. Auto MPG uses numeric columns; the original car-name field is omitted. Both datasets are loaded from a pinned Rdatasets revision. Timings in the notebook are diagnostic only: Kumo model loading and caching, library overhead, and hardware make them unsuitable as a controlled speed comparison.

## So, does feature engineering still matter?

These results compare a pretrained tabular model with tuned classical baselines under a limited, transparent protocol. They can help motivate which approaches to investigate, but do not establish that one model family is generally superior.

Kumo looks like a useful candidate when I have a prepared table and want a strong predictive starting point without a long tuning exercise. It does not remove the need to question the data, ask for better observations, or decide what the model is for.

Rather than declaring one universal winner, I would ask: **what is the next useful improvement for this project?** It could be a new data source, a more informative feature, a regression whose assumptions I can defend, or a faster model that fits the service budget. Sometimes it will be Kumo. The benchmark score is one input to that decision, not the decision itself.
